quotes.text: The thing most people miss is governance is a workload, not a feature. ASEs don't give you life cycle out of the box. Owners leave, cards keep surfacing.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Names the root cause of orphaned dashboard cards in one sentence.

quotes.text: Treat an ace like a UI skin, not an application. If the data matters, govern the system of record, not the card. If the process matters, push it into a platform with environments, ALM and policy enforcement.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a clear design rule for where data, process and UI belong.

quotes.text: This architecture scales because each layer owns one problem. Data is governed, policies enforced, UI is disposable. And when someone leaves, the group still owns it, the slot expires and your dashboard does not turn into a museum.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarises why the layered reference architecture survives turnover.

quotes.text: If a native surface exists that meets the need, default to that. Custom ACs are for format specialization, not for replacing first party features.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A pragmatic approval rule that prevents unnecessary custom development.

quotes.text: Does the data exist in a governed store under a standard contract with labels and retention? And does the ace only read and render? If yes, green. If no, it's not a card. It's a project.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Condenses the whole decision tree into a two-question test.

takeaways: Adaptive Card Extensions are a distribution layer, not an application, so data, ownership, placement and lifecycle must be governed underneath the card.

A governed reference architecture uses Entra ID groups, separate environments, canonical data contracts in SharePoint or Dataverse, Purview labels, CI/CD deployment and telemetry so cards stay disposable.
Approve a card only when it reads from a governed store under a standard contract, has two owners, lifecycle dates, a scoped placement and a rollback path; otherwise route it to a real project.
hook: Quick Adaptive Card Extensions in Teams and Viva Connections look harmless in demos but turn dashboards into a graveyard of orphaned, unlabeled cards. This episode is for Microsoft 365 architects, SharePoint and SPFx developers and governance owners who need a reference architecture, a decision tree and a checklist to approve or block card requests without becoming the villain.
